To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
flagging and walking samples are biased, that dry-ice tick traps are biased toward lone-star ticks, and that collecting from hosts can detect ticks that do not quest.
flagging, collecting ticks from the investigator's body, and trapping with dry- ice are all useful methods for sampling ticks, but each is biased by a different mechanism.

(1) flagging is a good method for sampling questing Ixodes dammini and Amblyomma americanuum ticks; (2) flagging is not a good method for collecting I. dammini ticks from leaf litter and ground vegetation; (3) walking is a good method to estimate risk of human encounter with I. dammini; and (4) trapping with dry ice is a useful method for collecting A. americanum ticks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of methods for sampling ticks in the environment.
the development of methods for the study of tick-borne disease.
developing sampling methods that are accurate and efficient for estimating tick population density, tick-borne pathogen prevalence in ticks, and human exposure to ticks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
no one sampling method is best for all purposes.

walking samples are the best for estimating risk to humans, flagging is better than walking for sampling ticks in leaf litter and low vegetation, and traps are better than flagging for sampling ticks on the ground.
flagging and trapping are useful methods for estimating the density of questing ticks, and flagging and walking are useful for estimating the human risk of tick-borne disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

flagging and walking samples are useful for estimating the risk of tick bites and the prevalence of pathogens in questing ticks, and that tick traps are useful for between-habitat and between-species comparisons.

walking and flagging are the most useful methods for comparing the relative distribution of tick species and life stages, but trapping and collecting from hosts are more useful for estimating tick abundance and pathogen prevalence.

flagging is a useful method to detect tick populations and that flagging, trapping, walking, and collecting ticks from favored hosts all have unique strengths and weaknesses that must be considered when planning a sampling strategy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
different sampling techniques are needed to answer different questions about tick populations.
the best method for sampling ticks depends on what you are trying to learn.
different tick sampling techniques are useful for different types of research questions, so researchers should carefully consider which method is most appropriate for their particular study.
